description: How audiences are segmented by demographic, psychographic and geographic variables, and how BARB and RAJAR measure them.
content_html:
Why Categorise Audiences?

Media organisations cannot sell advertising space or justify production budgets simply by saying “lots of people watch this.” Advertisers want to know which people — their age, income, values and habits. This is why the media industry invests heavily in audience research and categorisation. Three main types of segmentation are used: demographic segmentation, psychographic segmentation, and geographic segmentation.

The NRS Social Grade System

The most widely used demographic tool in UK media is the NRS social grade system, developed by the National Readership Survey and also used by JICNARS. The six grades are:

  • A — higher managerial, administrative or professional occupations (e.g. senior managers, doctors, solicitors)
  • B — intermediate managerial, administrative or professional occupations (e.g. teachers, nurses, junior managers)
  • C1 — supervisory, clerical and junior managerial occupations (e.g. office supervisors, sales staff)
  • C2 — skilled manual workers (e.g. electricians, plumbers)
  • D — semi-skilled and unskilled manual workers
  • E — those at the lowest levels of subsistence, including long-term unemployed and state pension recipients

Grade A and B individuals are often grouped as “ABC1” to describe an affluent, educated demographic; C2DE describes a working-class, lower-income grouping. These labels appear constantly in media planning documents and advertising rate cards.

Key Fact

The NRS social grades run from A (higher managerial and professional) to E (those at the lowest subsistence level). Grade A is not simply “wealthy” — it is defined by occupation type, not income level alone. This is the UK’s standard demographic segmentation tool for media audiences.

Psychographic Segmentation

Demographic data tells you who audiences are; psychographic data tells you how they think and what they value. Several frameworks exist. Young and Rubicam’s 4Cs model divides consumers by motivation. In the UK, the Values, Attitudes and Lifestyles (VALS) framework and variations on it have been applied to audience planning. Psychographic profiling allows an advertiser to target not just who a person is, but why they might want a product — their aspirations, anxieties and identity markers.

A streaming service launching a new nature documentary, for example, might target a psychographic profile defined by curiosity, environmental concern and cultural aspiration rather than simply by age or income bracket. The content and marketing would then be calibrated to speak to those values.

Digital platforms have moved beyond traditional segmentation by collecting first-party data — detailed records of what individual users actually watch, click, pause and search for. This behavioural data is far more granular than any demographic or psychographic category. A streaming platform knows not just that a user is a 28-year-old urban professional, but that they always finish crime dramas on weekday evenings, abandon romantic comedies after 20 minutes, and start a new series every 12 days. Those behavioural signals drive recommendation algorithms and inform commissioning decisions.

BARB: Measuring Television Audiences

The most authoritative television audience measurement in the UK is conducted by BARB (the Broadcasters’ Audience Research Board). BARB recruits a panel of households across the UK whose viewing behaviour is monitored electronically via meters on television sets and devices. The panel is designed to be statistically representative of the UK population. Data is collected daily and reported the following day as overnight ratings, with consolidated figures (including catch-up viewing) reported later.

The figures BARB produces — reach and share — are the currency of television commissioning and advertising sales. A drama that achieves a high overnight rating justifies its production cost; a low share on a Friday night might indicate poor scheduling rather than poor content.

Key Fact

BARB (Broadcasters’ Audience Research Board) measures UK television viewing using a representative household panel. It reports two key figures: reach (total viewers of a broadcast) and share (the percentage of the television audience watching a particular channel at a given time).

RAJAR, Pamco and Nielsen

RAJAR (Radio Joint Audience Research) performs the equivalent function for radio. Participants complete listening diaries over a set period recording what they listened to, when, and for how long. RAJAR data informs advertising rates and scheduling decisions across BBC and commercial radio.

Pamco (previously known as NRS) measures readership and reach for magazines and newspapers, while Nielsen provides global audience data including digital and streaming metrics. Together these bodies provide the quantitative evidence that underpins the entire commercial media economy.

BARB and RAJAR produce quantitative research — numbers and percentages that allow broadcasters to compare performance and set advertising rates. But numbers alone do not explain why audiences watch, what they enjoy, or how they feel. Qualitative research methods such as focus groups and in-depth interviews give richer insight. A film studio might commission quantitative research to discover how many 16–24-year-olds saw a trailer, and qualitative research to discover whether they found it exciting or confusing.
exam_tip_html: When discussing audience categorisation, be precise about which segmentation method you are using — demographic, psychographic or geographic. A common mistake is using “demographic” as a catch-all for all forms of categorisation. In longer answers, show you understand why a particular method was chosen: a luxury car advertiser and a fast-food brand will use the same NRS system differently because they are targeting different social grades for different reasons.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Audiences are categorised by demographic (who they are), psychographic (what they value) and geographic (where they live) segmentation; the NRS social grades A–E are the UK’s standard demographic tool, defined by occupation not wealth.
  • BARB measures UK television audiences using a representative household panel; RAJAR measures radio listening; Pamco covers print; Nielsen covers digital — collectively they provide the quantitative data underpinning commercial media.
  • Quantitative research provides viewing figures and reach; qualitative research — through focus groups and interviews — explains audience motivation and response.

practice_questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes NRS social grade A?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct answer is C. A) Incorrect — D and E describe semi-skilled and unskilled workers. B) Incorrect — C2 describes skilled manual workers. C) Correct — grade A is higher managerial, administrative or professional. D) Incorrect — this describes grade B.

practice_questions.text: Identify the organisation responsible for measuring television viewing figures in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: BARB (Broadcasters' Audience Research Board). Award mark for either the abbreviation or the full name.

practice_questions.text: Identify psychographic segmentation and explain one advantage it has over demographic segmentation for media producers.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: 1 mark for defining psychographic segmentation as dividing audiences by attitudes, values, interests and lifestyles. 1 mark for a developed advantage — for example, it allows targeting based on motivation and identity rather than just measurable social characteristics, meaning marketing can speak directly to why a person might want the product.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between 'reach' and 'share' as audience measurement terms.
practice_questions.marks: Developing: Gives a basic distinction between the two terms without precise definitions. Secure: Accurately defines reach as the total number of viewers of a broadcast and share as the percentage of the television audience watching a particular channel at a given time. Mastering: Accurate definitions plus a developed explanation of how each figure is used differently by the industry — for example, share reveals competitive performance against other channels at the same time, while reach is more important for demonstrating total audience size to advertisers.

practice_questions.text: Explain how BARB collects audience data and why this data is important to commercial television broadcasters.
practice_questions.marks: Developing: Shows basic awareness that BARB measures viewing but explanation is limited or inaccurate. Secure: Correctly explains that BARB uses a representative household panel with electronic meters, collecting daily viewing data; explains that this informs advertising rates and commissioning decisions. Mastering: Full, accurate explanation of the BARB methodology plus a clear account of two or more ways the data is used commercially (advertising rates, scheduling, programme commissioning) with a precise explanation of why the representativeness of the panel is important for credibility.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the different methods of audience categorisation help a media organisation to target and sell advertising to a specific audience.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Names one or two segmentation methods with limited explanation. Developing: Describes two methods with some explanation of how they are used, but links to advertising are vague. Secure: Explains demographic, psychographic and/or geographic segmentation clearly and shows how each type of data serves a different purpose for advertisers; references a named audience research body. Mastering: Sustained analytical argument explaining how the three segmentation types work together — for example, how NRS grades define the demographic target, psychographic profiling refines why they would respond to the product, and geographic data determines where to run the campaign; connects to the commercial logic of advertising rates and audience measurement.

glossary_terms.definition: Dividing audiences according to measurable social characteristics such as age, gender, ethnicity, education and income.
Dividing audiences according to their attitudes, values, interests and lifestyles.
Dividing audiences according to where they live, from country and region down to postcode.
A UK audience classification system dividing the population into six grades (A, B, C1, C2, D, E) based on the occupation of the chief income earner in the household.

Young and Rubicam's psychographic model dividing consumers into four main categories based on values, motivations and attitudes: Mainstreamers, Aspirers, Succeeders and Reformers (plus cross-category types).
Data collected directly by an organisation about its own users, based on their actual behaviour on that platform.
The Broadcasters' Audience Research Board, the organisation responsible for measuring television viewing figures in the UK.
The total number of people who watch at least some of a broadcast, expressed as an absolute number or percentage of the population.
The percentage of people watching television at a given time who are watching a particular channel.
Radio Joint Audience Research, the organisation that measures radio listening audiences in the UK.
An international audience measurement company providing data on digital and online audience behaviour.
Research that measures audiences in numbers, such as viewing figures, reach and share percentages.
Research that explores audience attitudes, experiences and motivations through methods such as focus groups and interviews.
